label: Argo
rationale: The debut and defining statement of the Jazztet, the Art Farmer/Benny Golson sextet that set the standard for arranged hard bop at the turn of the 1960s. AllMusic calls it 'an essential hard bop title' and says the band's reputation 'could rest on this stunning disc alone' (S2); Wikipedia reports a five-star AllMusic rating and a hit single, 'Killer Joe', which sold over 40,000 copies by August 1960 (S1). Golson's writing here — 'Killer Joe', 'I Remember Clifford', 'Blues March', 'Park Avenue Petite' — became repertoire. Session gravity is exceptional: McCoy Tyner's piano chair (his first major recording exposure before joining Coltrane later in 1960), Curtis Fuller, and the Farmer brothers, with Lex Humphries — a direct bridge into musicians already load-bearing in the canon.

ballot.album: Art Farmer-Benny Golson Jazztet — Meet the Jazztet (1960)
ballot.case_for: The debut and defining statement of the Jazztet, the sextet that set the benchmark for arranged three-horn hard bop; AllMusic calls it 'an essential hard bop title' whose band's reputation 'could rest on this stunning disc alone' (S2), with a five-star rating and a hit single in 'Killer Joe' (40,000+ copies by August 1960, S1) that became a standard. The album is a composer's showcase: 'Killer Joe', 'I Remember Clifford', 'Blues March', 'Park Avenue Petite' are all foundational repertoire in one place, and the tracklist's songfulness gives it real cold-listen discovery value. Session gravity is the strongest signal: McCoy Tyner's first major recording exposure months before joining Coltrane, plus Curtis Fuller alongside the Farmer brothers — a direct lineage bridge into musicians already load-bearing in the canon.
ballot.case_against: The consensus evidence is narrower than the rationale implies: AllMusic is the only substantive critical appraisal, S1 largely mirrors it, S3 is a sessionography, and S4/S5 are bare identifiers — no Penguin core listing, no NPR/JazzTimes/DownBeat canon citation, no independent musician citations in the dossier. The defining-statement case is partly overstated: 'I Remember Clifford' and 'Blues March' were already established via Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, leaving 'Killer Joe' as the only major piece genuinely introduced here, and some listeners will find the earlier Messengers versions more visceral. Finally, the Jazztet's polished, arranged sound is arguably a refined genre piece rather than a revolutionary statement, in an early-1960s hard-bop field already crowded with first-rank defining records.
ballot.disagreement: The references split on tier, not scope. Gemini reads the five-star AllMusic verdict, the 'Killer Joe' standard, and the Tyner debut as an overwhelming for-case meriting consensus_core; Deepseek holds that a single critical source (AllMusic, echoed by Wikipedia) with no Penguin/NPR/JazzTimes corroboration is too thin a consensus base, and that the repertoire-centrality claim is weakened by the Blakey precedents — hence contested. Both agree on priority 'strong' and both flag the same facts; they weigh them differently.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John treat this as a strong-but-contested candidate: clearly canon-worthy on repertoire, session gravity, and the Tyner lineage bridge, but held back from consensus_core until consensus evidence beyond AllMusic can be cited — include if the collection wants the definitive arranged-hard-bop statement.
